To choose correctly between “por” (cause, means, exchange, duration, agent) and “para” (purpose, recipient, deadline, opinion, comparison).
To use the structures “estar por + infinitive” and “para + ser/su edad” (para ser tu primer libro, para su edad).
To use the fixed expressions with “por” and “para”: por si acaso, por lo visto, por fin, por cierto, para nada, para colmo.
To use verbs with a fixed preposition: con (soñar, contar, casarse), de (acordarse, despedirse, depender), en (pensar, confiar, tardar), a (atreverse, acostumbrarse, negarse).
To avoid the traps: “to think about” = pensar EN, “to dream of” = soñar CON.

14 August, at Grandpa Gheorghe’s house in the country. Marta has come from Madrid for Grandpa Gheorghe’s birthday. She spent the whole night reading the first three chapters of Ecaterina’s book. Andrei leaves for Madrid in two weeks.
I read the three chapters last night, in one go. Ecaterina, this isn’t for a drawer. It’s for a publisher.
I don’t think so. I’m writing it for myself, in case I forget something.
For a first book, it’s very good. My editor dreams of publishing it in the spring. Can I count on you?
It depends on my eyes. And on whether I feel like it. It takes me a long time to write a page.
I’ll volunteer to take the cover photo. By the way, Marta, do you really not mind me living in your flat?
Not at all. I’ve got used to talking to myself, and that’s not good. Besides, the room has never been used: I painted it for you.
Thanks. My father has already asked how much I’m paying for the room.
Tell him nothing. That you’re paying in advance, in photos.
Andrei, do you remember what I told you in July?
That if I go mad, I should come back. I remember everything. But this time I’m not saying goodbye to anyone. I’m going for six months, not for forty years.
(laughing) Very good. You’ve learnt from my mistakes. That’s what old people are for.

“por” has a single syllable, with a short “r” at the end: [por]. “para” is stressed on the first syllable: PA-ra. In fast speech “para” is often reduced to “pa”: «pa’ ti», «pa’ casa» — understand it, but don’t write it.
It is linked into a single group, stressed on “ca”: [por-sia-KA-so]. “si” and “a” merge.
As with “volver”, the diphthong “ue” appears only under stress: a-cor-DAR-se, but te a-CUER-das, me a-CUER-do.
1. Por or para? B2 review
por
para
cause: Lo hizo por amor.
purpose: Lo escribo para recordar.
means: Hablamos por teléfono.
recipient: La habitación es para ti.
exchange, price: Pago 300 euros por la habitación.
deadline: Lo necesito para el lunes.
duration: Me voy por seis meses.
opinion: Para mí, es su mejor libro.
agent (passive): Fue escrito por Marta.
comparison: Para su edad, escribe muy bien.
approximate place: Paseamos por el pueblo.
direction: Salgo para Madrid mañana.
Trick: “por” looks BACK, to the cause (“because of what?”). “Para” looks FORWARD, to the purpose (“in order to do what?”, “for whom?”).
2. Structures and fixed expressions
The room has never been used yet. (estar por + inf. = to be still to be done)
I’m taking a jumper, just in case.
Apparently, Grandpa already knew.
Do you mind? — Not at all.
We arrived late and, to top it all, it started to rain.
“Estar para + inf.” = to be about to: «El tren está para salir». “Estar por + inf.” = to be still to be done, or to be tempted to: «La cama está por hacer», «Estoy por llamarla».

Agosto en el pueblo

Grandpa Gheorghe turned ninety-six on 15 August, the feast of the Assumption, and the family decided to celebrate in his village, far from the heat of Bucharest. They invited the whole club. Marta arrived from Madrid on the 13th, just as she had promised in April, when she said goodbye to Grandpa with an empty bottle of țuică in her suitcase and a promise to come back and fill it again.

Costel drove them all in a minibus his company had lent him. It was the first time in thirty years he had carried people instead of goods, and he was so nervous he drove at fifty kilometres an hour and announced the bends aloud, like a tour guide. Marta sat glued to the window. She looked at the haystacks, the horses and carts, the houses with wooden roofs and the wells with buckets hanging from them, and photographed everything on her phone, because she said nobody in Madrid would believe it.

Grandpa Gheorghe was waiting for them at the gate, leaning on his stick, in a freshly ironed white shirt. He was about to turn ninety-six and had a memory that, according to him, only failed him for things that didn’t interest him. He recognised Marta at once. He called her “the Spanish girl from April”, took the empty bottle from her hands, held it up to the light and said that apparently in Madrid people drank very fast. Then he filled it himself, in front of everyone, with great ceremony.

He got on with Costel from the very first minute. He asked him about all the countries he had driven through, and Costel counted them off on his fingers: Hungary, Austria, Germany, Italy, France, Spain, Poland. Grandpa said he had seen the sea only once, in 1968, and had found it too big. Costel promised to take him in the lorry one day, so he could see the world. Grandpa replied that to see the world he already had the television; but to watch Costel drive, he would gladly go.

The house was made of wood, with a long porch, a well in the yard, a vine shading the entrance and, at the bottom of the garden, an enormous walnut tree Grandpa had planted the year he married. Marta was given the “good room”, the one used only for important guests, with handwoven rugs and a bed so high you needed a chair to climb into it. Marta said she had never slept in a bed with a ladder.

On the first night they had dinner under the walnut tree, at a long table made of planks, by the light of bulbs Mihai had hung from the branches. Grandpa asked Marta about Andrés, and Ecaterina translated. Marta told him how the end had been: peaceful, without pain, with a drawing by Rosa Elena on the bedside table. Grandpa listened in silence. Then he said that apparently good men are slow to leave and go without making a noise. He raised his glass and said, in a Spanish he had learnt that very afternoon: “Por Andrés.” Everyone drank to him.

The next morning, at six, Marta went out into the yard and found Ecaterina sitting under the walnut tree, writing by hand in a notebook. There was no good signal in the village and she hadn’t brought her computer. Marta asked if she could read what she had written so far. Ecaterina hesitated a long time. Then she went into the house and came back with a folder: she had brought the first three chapters printed out, just in case. She said she didn’t really know why, but something had told her to put them in her suitcase.

Marta spent the whole day in the hammock on the porch, reading. She didn’t speak to anyone. At lunchtime her eyes were red and she barely tasted Mrs Florica’s sarmale; Mrs Florica had come with Costel and took it as a personal insult until Ana explained why. In the afternoon, Marta went to find Ecaterina under the walnut tree and told her this wasn’t for a drawer but for a publisher, and that her editor in Madrid dreamed of publishing it in the spring.

Ecaterina was afraid. She said so plainly. She was writing in Spanish because she had lived that story in Spanish, but she was afraid of mistakes, of sentences that sounded like translations, of misplaced commas. Marta replied that her Spanish didn’t need corrections; it needed readers. Ecaterina said everything depended on her eyes and on whether she felt like it, and that it took her ages to write a single page. Marta replied that she could wait. That in her family, apparently, they were very good at waiting.

Rosa Elena, for her part, had appointed herself Marta’s Romanian teacher. She took her to the river with Ana and Mihai and, sitting on a stone, taught her words: “apă”, “pește”, “încă o dată”. She was a very strict teacher. When Marta mispronounced something, the little girl shook her head, made her repeat it and wouldn’t let her move on to the next word until it sounded right. Ecaterina, watching them from the bank, told Ana quietly that someone had corrected her pronunciation in exactly that way, many years ago, in the back room of a bookshop.

Meanwhile, on the porch, Costel studied for the DELE with touching seriousness. Grandpa Gheorghe sat next to him and asked him questions in Romanian: how do you say “fântână”, how do you say “nuc”, how do you say “gata”. Costel answered and Grandpa repeated the words aloud, very slowly, like someone tasting a wine. By the end of the day he had learnt two expressions, “salud” and “por fin”, and used them for everything. When someone arrived, he said “por fin”. When someone left, he said “salud”.

On 15 August, the feast of the Assumption, Grandpa put on his best suit and took Marta to the village church. The older women wore embroidered headscarves and black skirts, and the children white shirts with red patterns. Marta said that in Spain the day was celebrated too, with processions and street parties, but that she had never seen so many people sing without sheet music and without making a mistake. Grandpa explained, through Ana, that in the village songs weren’t learnt: they were inherited.

In the afternoon they celebrated the birthday. Mrs Florica had made a three-tier cake with cream and strawberries, and Carmen had sent a whole jamón from Madrid with a note: “For Ana’s grandpa, many happy returns.” Costel gave Grandpa a miniature lorry he had painted himself, with the words “La Lámpara” on the side, so he could travel with him without leaving the village. But Grandpa had decided that in his house presents couldn’t be given to just one person, so Rosa Elena got hers too. Andrei gave her a real camera, small and sturdy, “so you can be my competition”.

Ecaterina gave her a leather-bound notebook with her name engraved on it: “For writing your books.” Marta gave her a copy of her grandfather’s novel, the Spanish edition, signed by her and with a shaky line Andrés had written in June, on the good morning, without anyone knowing who it was for: “For the girl with the lorry.” Marta explained to Rosa Elena that she didn’t need to read it now. She should keep it, just in case, for when she was older.

When the moment came to blow out the candles, Grandpa said that at his age he no longer had the breath for so many and asked Rosa Elena to blow them out and make the wish for him. The little girl turned very serious. Mihai reminded her that she had to make it silently, because if she said it aloud it wouldn’t come true. She thought for a moment, blew out both candles, a nine and a six, at once and, ignoring everyone, said her wish aloud, in Spanish: “I wish that Lola’s lamp never goes out.” For a few seconds, under the walnut tree, nobody dared say anything. Then Grandpa, who hadn’t understood a word, said “por fin”, and everyone burst out laughing.

That night, the club gave Andrei his farewell present, although he had banned the word “farewell”. It was a notebook in which each of them had written a sentence for Madrid. Mrs Florica had also sewn him a camera strap with Romanian embroidery, red and black, so that, according to her, everyone in Madrid would know where he came from. Andrei put it on straight away. He said it was the most beautiful strap in Europe and that he wasn’t going to take it off even to sleep.

Grandpa Gheorghe had something for him too. He told him, with Ana translating sentence by sentence, that when he went off to war, very young, his mother gave him bread, salt and a piece of advice: “Don’t forget to come back.” Then he gave Andrei a little cloth bag full of soil from the garden, from under the walnut tree. “Just in case you miss the earth,” he said. Andrei laughed, but put the little bag in his camera case, next to the batteries, very carefully.

Just then, Marta’s phone vibrated. It was an email from the city council that had managed to get through despite the poor signal: the plaque on calle de las Huertas would be unveiled on 7 October, at twelve noon. Marta read it aloud, first in Spanish and then in the very clumsy Romanian she had learnt in April. Costel did his sums out loud: the exam was in November, so in October he could go. He said that for a plaque like that he would go to Madrid even on foot.

Later, when everyone was asleep, Ecaterina and Marta stayed on the porch, looking at the stars, which in the village could be seen as they couldn’t in any city. Marta asked whether she would translate the book into Romanian herself. Ecaterina said of course. That at last she would be translating an author she knew well, one she could argue with over every comma and call at three in the morning to complain. Marta said that sounded like a marriage. Ecaterina said no, it sounded like a translation.

On 16 August they went back to Bucharest. Grandpa saw them off at the gate, just as he had welcomed them, leaning on his stick. He told them to come back soon, because at his age you couldn’t count on many more summers. Marta promised to come back the following summer with Ecaterina’s book published. Grandpa thought for a moment and replied that, in that case, he would have to last another year. That, as far as he was concerned, it was a deal. And as the minibus pulled away, he raised his hand and shouted: “¡Salud!”

Marta stayed two more days in Bucharest, at Ecaterina’s. On the last evening, Ecaterina showed her the desk in her bedroom and opened the third drawer, the bottom one, which was now empty. She explained that her 1987 letter had lain there for almost forty years, under some old bills, so that she wouldn’t see it every time she opened the drawer. Marta ran her hand over the wood at the bottom, slowly, without a word. Then she asked permission to take a photo of the empty drawer. She said she would like to put it on the cover of the book, if Andrei thought it was a good idea.

The next two weeks went by very fast. Andrei packed three cameras, five lenses, the club’s notebook, Mrs Florica’s strap and the little bag of soil into two suitcases, and had almost no room left for clothes. His mother cried every time she saw him fold a T-shirt. His father made him a list, in writing and in order of importance, of everything he had to check before leaving the house. The first item on the list was: “Call your mother.” The last: “Enjoy yourself.”

On 31 August, at five in the morning, the whole club was at the airport. Andrei had said he didn’t want goodbyes, so nobody said goodbye: they said “see you later”, “see you at Christmas”, “see you on 7 October”. Rosa Elena gave him a new drawing: Andrei with his camera, in front of a green sign. Costel cried, of course, but this time he said it was from lack of sleep, because he had got up at three. Nobody believed him.

Señor Dan was the last. He shook his son’s hand, very formally, as if at a business meeting. Then, without letting go of his hand, he pulled him close and hugged him for a long time. He said nothing. Andrei went through security, turned round and, before disappearing, raised his camera and took a photo of all of them waving to him. Later he would say it was the first photo of his professional life, and the only one he would never sell.

Marta was waiting for him at Barajas with a handwritten sign that said “Official photographer”, and Carmen and Juan had come with her, with a bag of churros, just in case. From the airport they went straight to Lavapiés, where Carmen had made an enormous tortilla, with onion, to see with her own eyes that Andrei ate the whole thing. Andrei ate the whole thing. Carmen said that boy was going to live in Madrid for a long time, and Juan, who didn’t say much, added: at least until the next tortilla.

At two in the afternoon a photo arrived in the club’s group chat. It was the hallway of the flat on the calle del Prado: the green sign and, next to it, held up with a drawing pin, Rosa Elena’s drawing. Underneath, Andrei had written: “I’m home. For now.” That night, in Bucharest, Ecaterina opened her computer and began a new chapter. The first sentence read: “For Andrei, who left without saying goodbye, but giving notice.” Then she sat for a while thinking about him, about Madrid, about a lamp left on. And she went on writing until very late.
